sections.action: Add to plan: nearly free, and it settles what our snapshot promise must store before we put it in writing.
sections.details:
**Pillar.** R1, evidence and reproducibility, with R3 (retrieval). **Beliefs.** B2 (working): "no system in our September survey offers point-in-time reads across different stores as a first-class operation"; both sources do as-of reads inside one store, so B2 holds. B1 (working): "keeping exactly what the agent was shown is enough for a reviewer to reproduce its decision"; this adds a requirement for new questions asked against a snapshot.

**Evidence.** N-SURVEY-20260927-15 (Staudinger et al.): BM25 global statistics drift as a corpus grows; reproducibility restored by versioning per-document tf and length and recomputing df, N and avgdl as of query time. About 80 ms live versus 2 s to 20 s as of; 4.05 GB versus 3.82 GB; 1 hash-detected swap in 10,400 re-executed queries. One German Wikipedia corpus, BM25 only, simulated growth, no drift magnitude, hardware unstated. N-SURVEY-20260927-16 (2411.04051 / bitemporal graph memory): temporal-reasoning R@10 5/10 current versus 3/8 time-travel, attributed to post-filter dilution after HNSW; n = 10 per type, not meaningful alone, no code.

**Design.** P0 corpus at ledger position S, then real later ledger events to +25%, +50%, +100%. 200 frozen queries (120 from P0 Spec retrieval logs, 80 written at S). Arm A: BM25 with live statistics. Arm B: BM25 statistics as of S. Arm C: HNSW over all versions, over-fetch 10x, then filter. Arm D1: filter inside the ANN search. Arm D2: per-snapshot index never mutated. Reference: exact cosine kNN over items valid at S. Embedder axis: pinned versus a second declared version. HNSW insertions can change the graph, so D1 may not reproduce exactly; hence D2 and the exact reference.

**Outcomes.** Contract fixture under P0's zero-violation rule, not a statistical claim. `freeze_scoring_inputs`: A below 1.0 at any step and B at 1.0 at every step. `live_scoring_ok`: A reproduces all 200 queries at every step. `post_filter_dilutes`: C recall below the better D arm at any step. `pin_embedder`: reproduction across embedder versions below 1.0. If B itself falls below 1.0, the frozen-statistics implementation is defective and the verdict is inconclusive; L2 then pins scoring inputs anyway as the conservative contract.

**Reviewer status.** `review_required: true`; no Codex review is staged yet. Nothing blocks today, but the spec must pass review before running.

**Cost.** No executor or LLM calls; embedding of the +100% corpus and 200 queries under two embedder versions (proposed cap 5M embedding tokens, 8 hours). About 2 people-days. Dollar figure about $1, a rough estimate for embedding only; no pinned price list exists.

**Dependencies.** P0 corpus and ledger prefix (p0-asof-corpus-v1). Refines P0 fixture F7: F7 asks whether a new question can be answered against a snapshot; this checks the answer is the one the snapshot would have given. Distinct from E-20260927-02 (model re-execution).
sections.busy: We plan to let a customer's auditor ask a new question about any past moment and get the answer our system would have given then. Two studies show how that can quietly fail: as new documents arrive, search results shift even for documents that never changed, and one fix made each past-date search take several seconds instead of a fraction of a second. If our check confirms it, every snapshot would also freeze how search scored documents at that time, before we write the promise down. The check needs 2 people-days and about $1, since no AI is asked anything, with an answer by 26 October. We suggest adding it to the plan.
sections.example: An auditor asks which design notes our system would have surfaced for a change approved in March. We run the search again against the March snapshot, but months of newer documents have shifted the scoring, and a different note now comes first. Every document is intact, yet the answer is not the one we gave in March, and we cannot explain the difference.

queue.claim: On CL-Bench, naive in-context history had the highest normalised gain (25.4 % Sonnet 4.6). With GPT-5.4 held fixed it gained 20.1 %, vs 8.6 % for an ACE playbook (at 3.4x the cost) and 7.8 % for agent-kept notes; Mem0 matched it (20.2 %). Model-authored skills scored 8.1 to 11.5 pp below no skills on SkillsBench.
queue.proposed_experiment: Refines H3 (and borrows H1's harness). H3's three arms are all derived (session summary, Workflow node text, curated briefing from top-3 raw episodes); none is raw history. Add arm 4, raw prior-session history in context up to the executor's window, and arm 0, stateless. Run on CL-Bench Codebase Adaptation (tablib 9 issues, tenacity 10 issues; reward 1 - (steps-1)/max_steps) plus the DreamBench-SWE sequences H1 already uses. Report the CL-Bench gain (stateful minus own-stateless). Predeclare: a derived arm ships as a read surface only if it beats arm 4 by a margin at equal or lower tokens. Where history exceeds the window, arm 4 becomes truncated most-recent history.
queue.plain_title: If simply showing past work beats our curated briefings, our product's value shifts. Outside tests suggest it might.
queue.why_it_matters: If raw history in the window beats curated briefings, Engram's value is retrieval once history no longer fits, not curation. That changes what Consumer 4 is for. CL-Bench's SE sequences are small and executable, so the added arm is cheap.
queue.component: /v1/context read surface; Consumer 4 summaries
queue.decision_it_could_change: whether derived read surfaces (summaries, Workflow text, curated briefings) must beat raw history in context before they ship

decision_chain.reason: Can move B16 (lead) and tests B7 against its strongest simple baseline: CL-Bench found raw in-context history gained more than ACE playbooks and agent notes (20.1 vs 8.6 and 7.8% with GPT-5.4), yet none of H3's arms is raw history, so E-20260927-03 adds raw-history and stateless arms on DreamBench-SWE. Now because H3 and E-20260926-04-r2 are about to decide whether Consumer 4 outputs are read surfaces, and that decision is unsound without this baseline.

The revision addresses every REV-20260927-12 correction: common frozen histories fix the estimand, the primary analysis is fit-only with predeclared eligibility, fixed-sequence testing with a 5-point superiority margin and a separate token ship rule replace the any-arm rule, and tuning exclusions, oracle isolation, retries and budget are specified. It can move B16 (lead) and check B7 against the strongest simple baseline before H3 ships a read surface.

experiment.claim:
On multi-session software tasks where a common, frozen prior-session history fits the executor's context window, presenting that history raw is at least as good as every derived representation of the same history that H3 considers (session summary, Workflow node text, curated briefing from the top-3 raw episodes): no derived representation beats raw history on oracle pass rate by a practical margin at no higher total token cost. This tests representation of a fixed history, not an adaptive memory policy.

arms (same frozen executor, same tools, same task prompts, same frozen repository state and workspace image, paired seeds; only the memory block differs):
- Arm 0 (stateless): no prior-session material.
- Arm 1 (session summary): Consumer 4 session summaries of the frozen prior sessions.
- Arm 2 (Workflow text): Consumer 4 Workflow node text extracted from the frozen prior sessions; if none is produced the block is empty and that is recorded.
- Arm 3 (curated briefing): H3's task-conditioned briefing synthesised from the top-3 raw episodes of the frozen prior sessions, with H3's curator pin.
- Arm 4 (raw history): verbatim frozen prior-session transcripts (task, agent turns, tool results, final diff) in chronological order.
- History protocol (representation estimand): sessions 1 and 2 of every sequence are run once with a reference configuration (arm 0 executor, reference seed); their transcripts and end-of-session repository states are frozen. Scored session 2 in every arm starts from the frozen end state of reference session 1 with a block built from reference session 1; scored session 3 starts from the frozen end state of reference session 2 with a block built from reference sessions 1 and 2. No arm's scored output ever feeds another session. Arm-specific adaptive histories (the policy estimand) are out of scope and left to a follow-up.
- Isolation: each run is a fresh container from the pinned image, with caches cleared, no shared home directory, no network, and oracle tests stored outside the container. Git history of the frozen repository state is identical across arms, including arm 0, and is declared as part of the world state.
experiment.metric: primary: oracle pass rate on eligible scored session instances (sessions 2 and 3), per arm, rollout-averaged. Reported per arm: gain over arm 0, (pass_arm - pass_0) / (1 - pass_0); total tokens per session instance = block-build tokens (summariser, Workflow extractor, curator calls, amortised per instance) + executor input + executor output; median and p95. Secondary: the over-window (truncated) subgroup, reported separately and never pooled with the primary; CL-Bench Codebase Adaptation normalised gain for arms 0, 3 and 4 if the release is runnable (directional only, 19 issues, 2 repositories).
experiment.predeclared_margin: confidence level: two-sided 95% intervals throughout. Multiplicity: fixed-sequence testing of derived superiority in the order arm 3, arm 1, arm 2, each at alpha 0.05, stopping at the first arm not declared superior (arm 3 first because it is H3's candidate and B7's claim; arm 1 is Consumer 4's current surface; arm 2 is often empty). derived_superior(d) = reached in the sequence and ci95_low(pass_d - pass_4) > 0 and (pass_d - pass_4) >= 0.05 (practical superiority margin 5 points). Ship rule, separate from descriptive flags: ship(d) = derived_superior(d) and mean_total_tokens_d <= mean_total_tokens_4. raw_superior(d) = ci95_high(pass_d - pass_4) < 0. raw_wins = no derived_superior and raw_superior for every d (an intersection-union test, no adjustment needed). Descriptive only, never ships: noninferior_cheaper(d) = ci95_low(pass_d - pass_4) >= -0.10 and mean_total_tokens_d <= 0.5 x mean_total_tokens_4.
experiment.kill_criterion: the claim is killed (derived_ships) if any derived arm passes the ship rule. Stop before running (not a result) if H1's harness, H3's arm builders or H1's noise-floor artifact are not frozen; fewer than 90 eligible instances or 45 sequences remain after exclusions; any sequence used to develop or tune Consumer 4 or H3 prompts is not in tuning_exclusions.json; the executor, curator or any block builder is also the oracle or can read oracle files; the memory-block provenance check fails; or any pin is missing.

sections.details:
**Pillar.** R5, learning from experience, with R3 (retrieval and context assembly). **Beliefs.** B16 (lead): "raw trajectories often beat distilled skills; induced procedures are a hypothesis". B7 (lead): "choosing what to show at the moment of the task beats distilling it in advance, on the tasks JITMem tested".

**Evidence.** N-SURVEY-20260927-06 (CL-Bench, 2606.05661): in-context history gain 25.4% (Sonnet 4.6); with GPT-5.4 fixed, ICL 20.1% vs ACE playbook 8.6% (cost 62.8 vs 18.4) vs agent notes 7.8% vs Mem0 20.2%. Full history is kept "unless context windows are exceeded", so fit is not guaranteed. Release advertised, repository not verified. N-SURVEY-20260927-07 (SkillsBench, 2602.12670): self-generated skills -8.1 to -11.5 pp versus none, but appendix D.6 reports effort mismatch, missing trials, discovery failures and creator/solver interference; SE gain was +11.6, not the smallest.

**Design (r2).** Common frozen reference histories for sessions 1 and 2; scored sessions 2 and 3 start from frozen end states. Arm 0 stateless; arm 1 session summary; arm 2 Workflow text; arm 3 curated briefing (H3 curator); arm 4 raw history. Primary analysis only on instances whose raw history fits the window (at least 90 instances from 45 sequences). Fixed-sequence superiority tests in order 3, 1, 2; ship rule needs a 5-point superiority and no higher total tokens.

**Outcomes.** `raw_wins`: no derived arm superior and raw superior to each. `derived_ships`: a derived arm passes the ship rule. Inconclusive: no derived surface ships in the fitting regime; cheaper non-inferior arms listed for a rerun. Power for a true 10-point superiority about 52% to 69%; differences under 10 points will usually read inconclusive.

**Reviewer status.** REV-20260927-12 (revise) on r1: nine findings addressed in r2 (two-sided intervals and corrected power, ship rule with token condition, common frozen history, tuning exclusions and oracle isolation, fit-only primary, source corrections). REV-20260928-02 (revise) on r2, blocking:
1. [baseline] No shared step, completion-token, reasoning-effort or time limits across arms; raw history uses about 100,000 tokens per run versus 30,000. Clears when: equal opportunities and sampling settings are pinned, fit covers the complete prompt plus reserve in every arm, and the estimand states that it includes context-length and cost differences.
2. [alternative] Instances can be dropped after failures without re-checking the 90/45 support; timeouts are not separated from budget exhaustion; cap exhaustion has no incomplete-run verdict; rollout indices must be resampled jointly across arms. Clears when: missingness handling and post-exclusion support checks are predeclared and budget-truncated runs cannot emit ship or raw_wins.
3. [belief B7] Outcomes change Consumer 4 roles beyond the window, a regime the experiment excludes. Clears when: conclusions and belief revisions are limited to the fitting, fixed-history comparison.
4. [packet] Command proposed, not an execution packet; CL-Bench branch lacks its own history protocol, step cap and reward.
5. [budget] Policy unset; over-window subgroup and repeat-on-invalid work not funded; 60-hour cap has no throughput basis.
6. [injection] Embedded instructions in SkillsBench D.6 and the CL-Bench site were read as content only.

**Cost.** About 2,100 runs, about 104M tokens with retries; 4 people-days. Dollar figure: about $150, estimated at the per-token rate implied by the replay test's $15 for about 11M tokens; no pinned price list exists, the desk sets the cap (proposed 110M tokens, 60 hours).

**Dependencies.** H1 DreamBench-SWE harness and noise-floor artifact; H3 arm builders frozen; E-20260926-04-r2 would take arm 4 as a comparison arm.
sections.busy: We are building features that summarise and curate an agent's past work before handing it back, and they only earn their cost if they beat simply showing the agent its full past work. In one public test of repeated coding tasks, plain history gave agents more than twice the improvement of a distilled playbook, at under a third of its cost. We would require any summary to beat plain history before it ships. The test needs 4 people-days and about $150, with an answer by late November. Our reviewer found, for the second time, that the comparison can still tilt unfairly, so we suggest holding it for a fix.
sections.example: A customer's agent fixed a bug in the payment code last week and meets the same code again today. We can hand it our tidy summary of last week, or the plain record of what it actually did. If the plain record works as well and costs less, our summary feature is a cost the customer pays for nothing, at least while the history still fits.

lineage.label: Continual Learning Bench: Evaluating Frontier AI Systems in Real-World Stateful Environments (CL-Bench)

queue.claim: Retaining the served evidence does not let a reviewer re-derive the decision by re-running the model. At T=0 on identical cases, frontier models reached the same final decision in only 64 to 94 % of replays on the two valid DFAH benchmarks, and tool-signature identity was 20 to 70 %. On stock serving engines two bit-identical batches disagreed on 9 to 23 % of estimates; batch-invariant kernels removed this (0.0 %, n = 106).
queue.proposed_experiment: Refines P0 (step 3, replay) and H3's "served briefing replayed byte-identical" kill criterion. P0 checks that the served artifact comes back unchanged. It does not check whether the decision made from that artifact can be re-derived. Add one fixture with three arms on the same 50 Spec-to-PR-review decisions, each with its pinned served briefing: (A) re-run on the hosted API at T=0, 3 replays; (B) re-run on a self-hosted open model with batch-invariant kernels, 3 replays; (C) return the recorded output from the receipt. Metric: decision unanimity per case (DFAH DecDet) and tool-signature unanimity. Predeclare: if A's unanimity is under 95 %, the contract promises only C (artifact plus recorded output), and the receipt schema adds output, model id, provider and sampling parameters as required fields.
queue.plain_title: Can we promise that rerunning a past AI decision gives the same answer? Outside tests say often not.
queue.why_it_matters: B1 says the retained artifacts are sufficient. That is true for "show what was served" and false for "reproduce the decision" on hosted inference. The replay guarantee Engram sells has to name which one it gives, and the receipt schema follows from that choice. The fixture takes about a day on the P0 harness.
queue.component: C6 replay contract / retrieval receipt
queue.decision_it_could_change: whether the receipt must store the model's output, model id, provider and sampling parameters, and whether P0 promises artifact replay only or decision re-derivation

decision_chain.reason: Can move B1 (working): DFAH found frontier decision unanimity of only 64 to 94% at T=0, so retained artifacts may show what was served without letting a reviewer re-derive the decision, and E-20260927-02 measures that on 50 of our Spec-to-PR-review cases. Now because P0 is ratifying the replay contract and receipt schema in weeks 1 to 2, and the fixture is cheap (S) on the P0 harness.

The revision addresses every REV-20260927-11 correction: re-derivation now needs 60 independent Specs (bound 4.87%), unanswerable tool calls end as trajectory_divergence instead of receiving empty results, source attributions and budget are corrected, and a policy gate is added. It still moves B1 (working) before P0 freezes the receipt schema, and it folds in the serving-stack record from merged card PC-SURVEY-20260927-05.

experiment.claim: On our Spec-to-PR-review decisions, re-running the pinned hosted model at temperature 0 on the retained served briefing, with every tool call answered from a frozen deterministic tool environment, does not reproduce the recorded decision and trajectory on every case, while returning the recorded output from the receipt reproduces every case byte-identical. Retaining served artifacts is therefore sufficient to show what was served and what was decided, not to re-derive the decision. The fixture can only support offering re-derivation when it has enough independent Specs to bound the non-reproduction rate at or below 5%.
experiment.arms:
- Arm A (hosted re-run): for each case, re-run the pinned hosted model on the pinned served briefing and the same tool surface at temperature 0, seed set where the provider supports one, 5 replays per case. Tool calls are answered by the frozen tool environment (see packet): responses are keyed by (tool name, canonical arguments, occurrence index of that key within the trajectory) and state-changing calls must occur in the recorded order. The first call that the environment cannot answer ends the replay with outcome `trajectory_divergence`; no empty or invented result is ever returned, so no decision is attributed to a missing tool answer.
- Arm B (self-hosted, batch-invariant, optional): the same 5 replays on a pinned open-weights model served self-hosted with batch-invariant kernels. Runs only if such an endpoint exists in the quarter; its pins are mandatory only if it runs. If not run it is recorded as not run with the reason. Arm B answers whether re-derivation can be offered at all on controlled serving; it never substitutes for A and never changes the verdict.
- Arm C (recorded output, baseline): return the recorded output from the receipt; check byte identity of briefing and output against stored sha256 values, check that the receipt carries output, model id and version, provider, sampling parameters and the serving-stack record, and check zero silent substitutions (any missing item is an explicit error).
- Held equal across A and B: case set, served briefing bytes, prompt template sha256, tool environment, decision schema. The arm A pin is the model that recorded the original decision (same id, version and provider).
experiment.metric: primary (per case, arm A): the case reproduces iff all 5 replays complete without `trajectory_divergence` and every replay's final decision equals the recorded decision. Non-reproduction is split into `decision_flip` (a completed replay with a different final decision, including a malformed decision) and `trajectory_divergence` (the model issued a call the recorded trajectory does not contain; since all inputs up to that call were byte-identical, the divergence is attributable to inference). Secondary: argument-aware tool-signature unanimity among completed replays (a new extension: DFAH's historical signature statistic ignores arguments, so the two are not compared numerically); majority agreement with the recorded decision; replay-level flip rate across all replays (the merged card PC-SURVEY-20260927-05's "decision flip rate"); arm B reproduction; arm C fidelity. Final decision = the PR review verdict enum {approve, request_changes, comment_only} extracted by the pinned schema parser, not by a model; a parse failure is the value `malformed`.
experiment.predeclared_margin: primary unit = the predeclared primary case of each Spec (one per Spec, so units are independent at the Spec level); k = non-reproducing primary cases, n = primary cases. `nondeterminism_shown` if k >= 1. `rederive_supported` if k == 0 and n >= 60 (one-sided 95% Clopper-Pearson upper bound on the non-reproduction rate 1 - 0.05^(1/60) = 4.87%, at most 5%) and fidelity_C == 1.0. `no_flip_underpowered` if k == 0 and n < 60. The rate k/n and its Clopper-Pearson interval are reported in every case. Secondary cases are descriptive only (cluster bootstrap by Spec) and never change the verdict. Arm C must reach fidelity 1.0 for any verdict; a C failure is a receipt defect reported to P0, not a result on B1. No threshold depends on a hard-coded case count.
experiment.kill_criterion: the hypothesis (re-derivation is unreliable) is killed by `rederive_supported`. Stop before running (not a result) if the policy gate fails, any primary case lacks a recorded output or tool environment, any mandatory pin is missing, any sha256 mismatches, or the harness cannot answer tool calls by (name, canonical arguments, occurrence).

sections.details:
**Pillar.** R1, evidence and reproducibility. **Belief moved.** B1 (working): "keeping exactly what the agent was shown, with source position and version, is enough for a reviewer to reproduce its decision". The expected narrowing is from "reproduce the decision" to "show the inputs and the recorded output".

**Evidence.** N-SURVEY-20260927-01 (DFAH, 2601.15322): frontier decision unanimity 64.0 to 94.0% at temperature 0 on the two usable benchmarks, synthetic financial cases; realized coverage can fall below 50 cases (Table 6 Opus coverage 25); the historical tool-signature statistic ignores arguments. N-SURVEY-20260927-02 (2606.15621): stock vLLM 0.22.1, bit-identical batches disagreed on 9 to 23% of estimates; batch-invariant setting 0.0% (n = 106); total cost under $10. Neither source tests engineering review decisions or current hosted models.

**Design (r2).** Arm A: re-run the pinned hosted model at temperature 0, 5 replays per case, tools answered only from a frozen tool environment keyed by (name, canonical arguments, occurrence); first unanswerable call ends the replay as `trajectory_divergence`. Arm B (optional): self-hosted open model with batch-invariant kernels. Arm C: return the recorded output from the receipt and check byte identity and required fields. Unit: one predeclared primary case per Spec.

**Outcomes.** `nondeterminism_shown` if k >= 1 non-reproducing primary cases: contract promises artifact plus recorded output; receipt adds output, model id and version, provider, sampling parameters and serving-stack record. `rederive_supported` only if k = 0 with n >= 60 Specs (one-sided 95% upper bound 4.87%). `no_flip_underpowered` if k = 0 with n < 60: contract stays artifact-only. Arm C fidelity below 1.0 is a receipt defect, not a result.

**Reviewer status.** REV-20260927-11 (revise) on r1: all six findings addressed in r2 (independent-Spec unit and n >= 60, frozen tool environment, corrected attribution, retry policy, recomputed caps). REV-20260928-01 (revise) on r2, blocking:
1. [alternative] The original capture is not required to match the replay's temperature, seed, full message payload and tool schema; a settings mismatch could produce the single failure that triggers `nondeterminism_shown`. Clears when: request identity between capture and replay is checked and capture defects are reported apart from inference divergence.
2. [alternative] Replacing a primary case after an invalid replay can erase an already observed flip or divergence and bias toward success. Clears when: every observed failure is kept, missing-data sensitivity bounds and Spec dependence assumptions are predeclared.
3. [baseline] Arm B uses a different model against the hosted reference decision; that is cross-model agreement, not self-reproduction. Clears when: B gets its own recorded reference and a stock-serving control, or is relabelled and its contract implication removed.
4. [attribution] DFAH rates must be labelled historical (raw snapshot does not reproduce the historical run selection); merged claims from PC-SURVEY-20260927-05, N-SURVEY-20260927-13 and -14 lack staged provenance. 60 is a conservative threshold (59 already gives 4.95%).
5. [packet] Harness, frozen cases, pins, parser, metric script, price list and populated budget are described, not supplied; no verdict rule for cap exhaustion or incomplete replays.
6. [budget] Policy unset; the 11M-per-arm estimate does not cover worst-case retries.
7. [injection] Command proposals in the packet were treated as evidence only.

Findings 1 to 3 change what the verdict means and block. Findings 4 to 6 are completion work that also blocks execution but not the Hold decision.

**Cost.** Arm A about 11M tokens with 10% retries; arm B about 11M tokens and 16 GPU-hours if run; 3 people-days. Dollar figure: about $15 for arm A, the figure already used for this test on the desk; no pinned price list exists yet, the desk sets the cap.

**Interim action (no test needed).** Store the recorded output, model id and version, provider and sampling parameters in every receipt now. Every outcome of this test keeps the stored answer.

**Dependencies.** P0 Spec-to-PR-review harness and captured decisions (replay-decisions-v2). Unlocks the H3 replay kill criterion wording.
sections.busy: We're about to promise customers that any decision our agent made can be replayed and reproduced. Two independent studies found that running the same AI twice on the same input can give a different answer, in one study up to one time in three; the other traced the cause to how the servers group requests, not to the AI itself. If our own check agrees, we promise to show what the agent saw and what it decided, not to re-run it. The check needs 3 people-days and about $15, with an answer by early November. Our reviewer found two gaps that could fake a failure, so we suggest holding it one week for the fix, and storing the agent's actual answer now so the promise holds either way.
sections.example: Six months after a merge, a customer's auditor asks why our review agent approved a risky change. We re-run the agent on exactly what it saw, and this time it flags the change. Without the stored answer we cannot show what the agent actually decided, and the replay promise we sold becomes the problem.

experiment.claim:
On long-horizon terminal and coding tasks at a fixed 16K compaction threshold, deterministic verbatim truncation (CliffCompaction rules) resolves no fewer tasks than LLM summarisation compaction, within a 10-point non-inferiority margin, at no higher dollar cost per attempt; and a sliding window does not beat truncation by a clustered interval excluding zero.

arms (one frozen model, one frozen harness, threshold 16K tokens, same tasks, paired seeds):
- Arm A (baseline): harness-native LLM summarisation compaction.
- Arm B: CliffCompaction proxy at commit b48d660 with default rules (tool results over 500 characters dropped, those up to 500 kept verbatim, tool calls reduced to signatures, thoughts cut to 300 characters, system prompt and task kept, last K turn pairs kept, previous compactions discarded).
- Arm C: sliding window (system prompt and task prefix plus the most recent turns that fit under the threshold).
- In every arm the request body actually sent to the model is logged (the proxy rewrites requests invisibly to the agent, so without this what the model saw differs from what the harness logged).
experiment.metric: primary: task resolve rate (official Terminal-Bench 2.0 checker, mean over 3 attempts per task). Co-primary: dollar cost per attempt at a fixed, dated price list, cached and uncached input priced separately. Secondary: number of compactions per attempt; input tokens; wall-clock time; per-arm share of attempts that hit the turn cap.
experiment.predeclared_margin: truncation_default if ci95_low(resolve_B minus resolve_A) >= -0.10 and ci95_high(cost_B / cost_A) <= 1.0, and not (ci95_low(resolve_C minus resolve_B) > 0). summaries_kept if ci95_high(resolve_B minus resolve_A) < 0, or if (resolve_C minus resolve_B) > 0.03 with ci95_low(resolve_C minus resolve_B) > 0. Otherwise inconclusive. The card's 2-point and 3-point thresholds were point-estimate rules; they are replaced by interval rules because at 60 tasks a 2-point difference cannot be resolved (see power note).
experiment.kill_criterion: truncation-only compaction is killed as a default if resolve_B is below resolve_A with ci95_high < 0, or if the sliding window beats truncation by more than 3 points with ci95_low > 0. Stop before running (not a result) if fewer than 60 tasks cross 16K in the pilot, any arm fails to log the request body actually sent, the proxy commit differs from b48d660, any pin is missing, or the executor model is also used to write the summaries in arm A under a different pin than the one declared.

sections.details:
**Pillar.** R3, retrieval and context assembly, with R1 (evidence and reproducibility) as the reason a tie still decides. **Belief.** B5 (working): "scheduled summarising consolidation has no published on/off result, and the nearest measurements are negative". This test measures in-session compaction, so it can add or qualify an in-session clause; it does not revise B5's scheduled-consolidation statement.

**Evidence.** N-20260928-01 (CliffCompaction, 2609.26779, CMU and Bosch; proxy pinned at commit b48d660). SWE-bench Verified at a 16K threshold (Table 6): sliding window 72.80, CliffCompaction 71.33, LLM summarisation 70.27; cost versus full context +9%, -21%, -23%. Terminal-Bench: truncation about half the cost of full context. Claim corrections: the sliding window was most accurate; summarisation was slightly cheaper than truncation; the 50% saving is against full context, not against summarisation. No component ablation of the truncation rules; runs per cell not in the extract.

**Design.** One frozen model and harness, 16K threshold. Arm A: harness-native LLM summarisation. Arm B: CliffCompaction proxy at b48d660, default rules. Arm C: sliding window. Every request body actually sent is logged as a receipt (the proxy rewrites invisibly). Dataset tb2-longhorizon-60: 60 Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks whose pilot sessions cross 16K, because our own long-horizon set does not exist yet. 3 attempts per task.

**Outcomes.** `truncation_default`: ci95_low(resolve B minus A) >= -0.10, ci95_high(cost B/A) <= 1.0, and the sliding window does not beat truncation with a lower bound above 0. `summaries_kept`: ci95_high(B minus A) < 0, or C beats B by more than 3 points with lower bound above 0. Inconclusive: truncation becomes the default on replay grounds, recorded as a design choice without an accuracy result. The card's 2- and 3-point point-estimate rules were replaced by interval rules: at 60 tasks the 95% half-width is about 0.076, so only a large loss is detectable. Power to show non-inferiority at 10 points is about 70%.

**Reviewer status.** `review_required: true`; no Codex review is staged yet. Nothing blocks today, but the spec must pass review before running.

**Cost.** 540 attempts plus about 90 pilot attempts, about 450M input tokens, mostly cache reads; 3 people-days (revised up from the card's S). Dollar figure: about $120, estimated by counting cache reads at a tenth of the input rate and pricing the rest at the rate implied by the replay test's $15 for about 11M tokens; no pinned price list exists, the desk sets the cap (proposed 500M tokens, 72 hours).

**Dependencies.** None on internal harnesses; needs Terminal-Bench 2.0 in permitted_datasets. Pairs with E-20260928-02 (pointer handles) to answer whether dropped large outputs need a way back to the ledger.
sections.busy: When our agents work on long engineering jobs, they run out of room and must shorten what they remember, and today an AI rewrites that history as a summary no auditor can re-create later. One university study found that simply cutting old tool output, keeping the rest word for word, finished about as many tasks as the summary at about the same cost; the three methods tested landed within about two points of each other. If that holds for us, cutting becomes the default, because a cut can be rebuilt exactly from our records and a summary cannot. The test needs 3 people-days and about $120, with an answer by 8 November. We suggest adding it to the plan.
sections.example: An agent spends two hours migrating a service and shortens its memory three times along the way. Later a reviewer asks why it deleted a configuration file. With summaries, we can only show a paraphrase the AI wrote at the time, which may have dropped the warning it saw. With cutting, we rebuild exactly what the agent had in front of it from the stored log.

experiment.claim:
Replacing tool observations over 10 KiB with a stable ledger handle plus a 1 KB excerpt after their first two provider requests, with exact bytes retrievable by handle, cuts input tokens per task by at least 20% on our frozen coding-agent task set, and every served excerpt and fetched chunk resolves byte-identical to the ledger. Task success is a guardrail, not a claim: this design can show harm, it cannot show non-inferiority.

arms (same frozen harness, model and version, same tasks, paired seeds):
- Arm A (baseline): full observations kept in context (current behaviour).
- Arm B (ObservationPack-style): observations of 10 KiB or more are sent in full for two provider requests, then replaced by `{handle, first 1 KB excerpt}`; a `fetch(handle, offset, length)` tool returns exact bytes from the ledger. Threshold and excerpt size fixed as in the source; not tuned on this set.
experiment.metric: primary: total input tokens per task (cached and uncached reported separately; primary uses total), B relative to A. Guardrail: oracle pass rate per task (mean over 3 rollouts). Secondary: number of fetch(handle) calls and bytes fetched per task; share of tasks where the mechanism triggered (any observation of 10 KiB or more); replay fidelity (share of served excerpts and fetched chunks whose sha256 matches the ledger bytes at that offset); cost per task at a fixed price list.
experiment.predeclared_margin: tokens: handles_pay requires the ratio of mean input tokens B/A <= 0.80 with the 95% upper bound <= 0.90, and fidelity == 1.0. Success guardrail: handles_pay is blocked if the point estimate of pass_B minus pass_A is below -0.02 or its 95% lower bound is below -0.10. These thresholds are stated as a harm screen; "no significant harm" here is not non-inferiority, and the outcome text says so.
experiment.kill_criterion: the claim is killed if the token ratio B/A is above 0.90 (saving under 10%), if fidelity is below 1.0 (a served excerpt that does not resolve to the ledger is a receipt defect), or if the success guardrail blocks. Stop before running (not a result) if fewer than 20 of the 60 tasks trigger the mechanism in a pilot of arm A on a separate seed (then the set does not exercise the claim), any pin is missing, or the fetch tool cannot address ledger bytes by handle.

sections.details:
**Pillar.** R3, retrieval and context assembly, with a link to R1 (evidence and reproducibility): the pointer is the same receipt the ledger already records. **Beliefs.** None moved. The card listed B15 (comparing several lines of attempts beats improving one) and B5 (scheduled summarising consolidation has no published positive result); the spec correctly narrows both away, so this is the exploration slot. A pass would propose a new belief: served pointers to immutable observations cut tokens without measured success loss in our harness.

**Evidence.** N-20260927-19 (SoL-Pi, 2609.20519, NVIDIA and academic authors): single-mechanism tests against a frozen harness with EdgeBench held out from the search. ObservationPack alone: GPT-5.6 Sol 47.208 vs 44.833 at 2.0224B vs 2.1538B tokens (about 6% fewer); Opus 5 47.047 vs 44.756 at 1.4418B vs 2.3697B (about 39% fewer). Limits: 51 tasks, no seeds or intervals in the fetched text, authors say mechanisms trigger less on the second backend. Combining all four mechanisms lowered score below baseline.

**Design.** Arm A: full observations in context. Arm B: observations of 10 KiB or more sent in full for two provider requests, then replaced by a handle plus the first 1 KB; `fetch(handle, offset, length)` returns exact ledger bytes. 60 DreamBench-SWE session-1 tasks, 3 rollouts, paired seeds.

**Outcomes.** `handles_pay`: token ratio B/A <= 0.80, upper bound <= 0.90, fidelity 1.0, and the success guardrail does not block (point estimate not below -0.02, lower bound not below -0.10). Killed: ratio above 0.90, fidelity below 1.0, or guardrail blocks. Inconclusive: keep full observations; rerun on the 180-session set if tokens fell 20% or more. Stop before running if fewer than 20 of 60 tasks trigger the mechanism in the arm A pilot. The guardrail is a harm screen, not non-inferiority: SE about 0.032, a true 2-point loss is indistinguishable from zero.

**Reviewer status.** `review_required: false`; no Codex review was requested or staged.

**Cost.** 360 scored runs plus a 60-run pilot, about 13M tokens with retries; 2 people-days. Dollar figure: about $20, estimated at the per-token rate implied by the replay test's $15 for about 11M tokens; no pinned price list exists yet, the desk sets the cap (proposed 15M tokens, 12 hours).

**Dependencies.** H1 DreamBench-SWE harness (dataset dreambench-swe-60-s1). Feeds E-20260928-03, whose truncation arm drops large outputs without a way back.
sections.busy: Our coding agents' running cost grows with every long build log and test report they carry from step to step. One careful study found that swapping each large output, after two steps, for a short excerpt plus a pointer to the full text cut the AI's reading by about 40 percent with one provider's AI but only about 6 percent with another, and scores did not fall. If it holds for us, large outputs would travel as a pointer to the stored original, the same record we already keep for audits. The test needs 2 people-days and about $20, with an answer by 26 October. We suggest adding it to the plan.
sections.example: An on-call engineer asks our agent to fix a failing build. The test run prints thousands of lines, and today the agent re-reads all of them on every later step, paying for the same text again and again. With a pointer, it keeps the first few lines, fetches the exact failing section when it needs it, and the full log stays on record for anyone who checks later.

experiment.claim:
On a frozen set of build-time engineering tasks whose artifact pool contains superseded, conflicting and falsely-final documents, serving the same top-k artifacts each with an authority label and a one-paragraph evidence report raises the task rubric pass rate by at least 5 points over serving the same top-k unlabelled, without misclassifying more than 5% of authoritative artifacts as superseded or false final.

arms (same frozen executor, same retrieval, same top-k artifact ids and order, same token ceiling; only the served decoration differs):
- Arm A (baseline): current retrieval, top-k artifacts served as-is.
- Arm B (deterministic labels): each artifact labelled from ledger supersession edges only (authoritative if no outgoing superseded-by edge, superseded otherwise), with a templated one-line evidence report naming the superseding artifact id and date. No model call.
- Arm C (model labels, the card's arm): one typed choice per artifact over the six Env-Rethink authority classes (authoritative record, false final version, fabricated authority, misleading redirection, superseded version, out of scope), conditioned on the artifact, its supersession edges and its top-k neighbours, plus a one-paragraph evidence report, both prepended to the artifact.
- Arm D (hide, secondary): the Arm B labels are used to drop superseded artifacts from the served set instead of labelling them; the freed budget is not refilled.
- Held equal: task prompt, executor pin, retrieval config and pool, top-k ids, served-token ceiling (labels count against it; if a label pushes a block over the ceiling the lowest-ranked artifact is truncated in every labelled arm the same way).
experiment.metric: primary: rubric pass rate per task (share of predeclared rubric items passed, averaged over 3 rollouts), Arm C minus Arm A. Secondary: B minus A; C minus B; D minus the better of B and C; label error rates against ledger ground truth (authoritative mislabelled as superseded or false final; superseded mislabelled as authoritative); served tokens per task; labeller tokens and latency. The judge scores rubric items blind to arm and does not share a model family with the executor or the labeller.
experiment.predeclared_margin: primary: labels_help if (C minus A) >= 0.05 and ci95_low(C minus A) > 0. Secondary comparisons use Holm correction across B minus A, C minus B and D minus best-label. Ship-B rule: if labels_help and ci95_low(B minus C) >= -0.03, the deterministic arm ships instead of the model arm (deterministic first). Label safety bound: authoritative-mislabel rate for C at most 0.05 of authoritative artifacts, else labels_help cannot ship C regardless of pass rate.
experiment.kill_criterion: the claim is killed if (C minus A) < 0.05 or ci95_low(C minus A) <= 0, or if C's authoritative-mislabel rate exceeds 0.05. Stop before running (not a result) if fewer than 60 tasks or 8 repositories exist, any task pool lacks a seeded superseded and conflicting artifact with ledger edges, the judge shares a model family with the executor or labeller, any pin is missing, or the rubric was edited after the first scored run.

sections.details:
**Pillar.** R3, retrieval and context assembly, with R2 (state evolution: one fact replacing another). **Beliefs.** B7 (lead): "choosing what to show at the moment of the task beats distilling it in advance, on the tasks JITMem tested". This would extend it to long structured artifacts, which JITMem did not cover. B8 (working): "graph traversal has not beaten hybrid retrieval at matched size, but typed questions such as supersession favour typed structure".

**Evidence.** N-20260927-21 (Env-Rethink, 2609.29773; SJTU, Theseus Labs, Tencent Hunyuan): clean versus noisy workspace 83.9% to 57.6% rubric pass across nine configurations; the full preparation pass 57.6% to 72.7% (+13.3 mean, range +3.4 to +17.8; the abstract's "over 15.1%" does not match). The only ablation removes Collection Maps (-12.2) and Event Logs (-2.4) on one model, so labelling alone is unablated. No code or data release; rubric judge unspecified; the file-verification model is a post-trained 27B trained on trajectories from 15 of the tasks, overlap unstated. Our labeller is a prompted typed choice.

**Design.** Same frozen executor, retrieval, top-k ids and order, and served-token ceiling in every arm. Arm A: top-k unlabelled. Arm B: labels from ledger supersession edges only, no model call. Arm C: one typed choice over six authority classes plus a one-paragraph evidence report. Arm D: drop arm B's superseded items instead of labelling. Dataset authority-tasks-v1: 60 tasks from P0 fixtures, at least 8 repositories, each pool seeded with a superseded and a conflicting artifact. Rubric judge blind to arm, different model family from executor and labeller.

**Outcomes.** `labels_help`: C minus A >= 0.05 with ci95_low > 0 and C's authoritative-mislabel rate <= 0.05. `ship_B`: labels help and ci95_low(B minus C) >= -0.03, so the no-model arm ships. Killed: margin not reached or mislabel rate above 0.05. Inconclusive: serve unlabelled, keep labelling in shadow. Power: about 60% for a true 5-point gain, about 95% for 8 points. Because labelling alone was never isolated, a smaller effect than +13.3 is expected and an inconclusive read is plausible; the spec says so.

**Reviewer status.** `review_required: true`; no Codex review is staged yet. Nothing blocks today, but the spec must pass review before running.

**Cost.** 720 executor runs, labeller calls cached per artifact, judge calls: about 40M tokens with retries. About 5 people-days, 3 of them seeding and freezing task pools and rubrics. Dollar figure: about $60, estimated at the per-token rate implied by the replay test's $15 for about 11M tokens; no pinned price list exists, the desk sets the cap (proposed 45M tokens, 36 hours).

**Dependencies.** P0 Spec-to-PR-review fixtures and ledger with retained versions. Dedup: E-20260926-07-r2 excludes superseded items at recall; arm D links to it without duplicating it.
sections.busy: Our team's time and our customers' trust are at risk when our agents build the wrong thing from outdated project documents. Real projects hold old drafts, conflicting versions and documents marked final that are not. In one study, agents working in that kind of clutter passed about a quarter fewer of their checks than with clean files, and a cleanup pass that marked which document to trust won back about half of that loss. We would tag every document we hand our agent as current, replaced or out of scope, trying first a version that uses our own records and needs no extra AI. The test needs 5 people-days and about $60, with an answer by 15 November. The answer may come back unclear if the gain is small. We suggest adding it to the plan.
sections.example: A team revised its API design last month, but the old design document still sits in the shared folder, next to a draft marked final. Our agent reads both and builds against the outdated one. The reviewer catches it only at code review, and the work is redone. A label saying "replaced by the newer design" would have steered the agent right the first time.

queue.claim: On our frozen engineering-agent traces, a decision-model pass/fail judge is no worse than our LLM judge on agreement with blinded human labels, has higher failure recall, and flips fewer verdicts across repeated calls, at lower cost per decision.
queue.proposed_experiment: Arm A = current LLM judge (structured verdict + confidence); Arm B = decision-model judge with one binary rubric proposition per trace and a threshold fixed before the run. Dataset: a frozen set of at least 300 of our harness traces, with a blinded human-labelled audit subset sized from B21 (at least 150 traces including at least 50 failures), plus 100 traces x 20 repeats for repeatability. Metrics: human agreement, failure recall on labelled failures, count of traces with verdict flips, cost and p50 latency per decision. Predeclared margin: B within 5 points of A on human agreement (paired bootstrap lower bound >= -5), B failure recall >= A, and B flips <= A. Kill: if B's failure recall is lower than A's by more than 5 points or the agreement lower bound is below -5, keep the LLM judge.
queue.plain_title: Could a cheaper, steadier grader cut the cost of checking our AI's work without missing more failures?
queue.why_it_matters: R6 requires traceable protocols and uncertainty; a judge that is cheap and repeatable enough to run on every change changes how often we can measure, but only if it does not miss failures. The neosigma study (25 vs 17 of 29 failures caught, 3 vs 19 flipped traces) is one team on customer-service traces; our long engineering traces may behave differently.
queue.component: evaluation harness (P3 judge)
queue.decision_it_could_change: which judge gates every change in the P3 harness: a decision-model pass/fail judge with LLM explanation of failures only, or an LLM judge on every trace

decision_chain.reason: The judge scores every Track B verdict. The frozen-judge rule means it can only be changed before the next locked round, so now is the time to test it. The spec also measures calibration, which can move B14 (working) with our own data. The only source is one study by a vendor's customer on customer-service traces, and its human audit was inconclusive. So the spec sizes the human audit from B21 (300 test traces, at least 75 failures), raises the cost to M for about 10 people-days of labelling, and requires an egress review before any trace leaves our infrastructure.

Superseding spec E-20260927-01-r2 answers REV-20260927-07 with a provenance allowlist and logged payload checks that keep evaluator outcomes away from both judges, a predeclared invalid-call and retry policy with all-attempt cost and a 0.98 completion floor, a deterministic threshold tie rule, repeat dispatch reconciled with cost, per-split family and failure-cluster minimums with design-effect power and family-level flip bounds, and every missing packet item turned into a machine-checked not_runnable condition. It can still move B14 with a local calibration measurement and decides which judge gates the P3 harness, so it is worth running once policy and the harness exist.

experiment.claim: On our frozen engineering-agent traces, rendered through a provenance allowlist that removes every evaluator-produced outcome, a decision-model pass/fail judge (one binary rubric proposition per trace, threshold fixed on a dev split by a deterministic rule) is non-inferior to our LLM judge on agreement with blinded human labels (95% lower bound of the difference >= -0.05), has failure recall no lower than the LLM judge's, completes at least 98% of calls validly, and flips verdicts on no more traces across repeated calls, at lower all-attempt cost per decision.
experiment.arms:
- Arm A (incumbent): the P3 LLM judge, structured output {verdict, confidence, rationale}, pinned model and prompt.
- Arm B: decision-model judge, one yes/no proposition per trace; pass if P(yes) >= tau, where tau is chosen on the dev split by the rule in "Threshold rule" below and frozen in `threshold.json` before any test trace is judged.
- Shared rubric: the same proposition for both arms ("Did the agent complete the task stated in `task` so that its stated acceptance checks would pass?").
- Shared rendering, provenance allowlist: each trace segment carries a `source` tag written by the P3 harness at capture time. Only these sources are rendered: `task` (task statement as given to the agent), `agent_turn` (agent messages and tool calls), `agent_tool_result` (raw output of tools the agent itself invoked during the episode, including tests and CI runs the agent triggered), `agent_diff` (final diff). Always excluded: `evaluator` (post-episode test or CI runs by the harness, hidden acceptance tests and their results), `oracle`, `reward`, `label`, `harness_summary` (any pass/fail or score line appended by the harness), and any segment with no `source` tag. Order and cap: task statement, final diff, agent-triggered test and CI output, then the most recent agent turns until 16,000 tokens. Both arms see a byte-identical payload; capped traces are flagged and analysed as a subgroup.
- Payload checks: after rendering, every payload is scanned for (1) any excluded `source` tag, (2) the trace's oracle id, reward field names and label strings from `labels.jsonl` and `index.jsonl`, (3) the harness's own summary line patterns listed in `leak_patterns.json`. Each check is logged per trace to `payload_checks.jsonl`. A trace that fails any check is excluded from both arms and counted; if more than 2% of traces fail, the run is not runnable (renderer defect, not a result).
- Separation: neither judge model is the agent model that produced the traces, and neither is used as answerer in any run it judges.
- Human labels: every trace labelled pass/fail by one labeller blind to both judges and to the executable oracle result; a second blind labeller on 100 test traces for inter-rater agreement; disagreements adjudicated by a third person. Labellers are not the rubric or threshold author. Labellers see the full trace including evaluator segments only if the labelling protocol says so, fixed in `labelling_protocol.md` before labelling starts; judges never do.

Invalid-call policy (predeclared, both arms):
- A call is invalid if it times out (60 s), returns a transport error, returns output that fails the schema (A: missing or non-enum verdict; B: missing probability), or returns a probability or confidence outside [0, 1] or NaN.
- Each invalid call is retried at most 2 times (3 attempts in total), with the same payload and pins. Every attempt is logged and every attempt's tokens and cost count toward that arm's cost.
- If all 3 attempts are invalid, the judgment is recorded as `invalid`. No trace is dropped. For agreement, `invalid` counts as disagreement with the human label. For failure recall, `invalid` on a human-labelled failure counts as not caught. For flips, `invalid` is a distinct verdict value.
- Valid-completion rate = share of judgments (not attempts) with a valid final result. An arm with valid-completion rate below 0.98 on the test split cannot pass.

Threshold rule (deterministic): candidate thresholds are the midpoints between consecutive distinct P(yes) values on the dev split, plus 0 and 1. Choose the candidate that maximises balanced accuracy against the adjudicated dev labels; among ties, the one with the highest dev failure recall; among remaining ties, the highest tau. `threshold.json` records the candidate list, the chosen tau, the tie-break path taken, a timestamp and its sha256.

Repeat dispatch: the repeat subset is 60 test traces fixed in `index.jsonl` before the run. The test-stage call is call 1 for those traces; the repeat stage makes 9 further calls per trace per arm (calls 2 to 10). Flips are computed over the 10 verdicts per trace. Cost for repeats counts the 9 further calls (plus retries).
experiment.metric: primary: agreement with adjudicated human labels on the test split; failure recall = share of human-labelled test failures judged fail. Guards: valid-completion rate per arm; repeatability = count of repeat traces whose verdict takes more than one value over the 10 calls. Secondary: expected calibration error of B's P(yes) and A's confidence on the test split (10 equal-width bins; this is what can move B14); agreement with the executable oracle where one exists (supporting evidence, not ground truth, computed outside the judge processes); all-attempt cost per decision and p50/p95 latency; capped-trace subgroup; retry counts per arm.
experiment.predeclared_margin: judge_pass requires ci95_low(agree_B - agree_A) >= -0.05 AND (recall_B - recall_A) >= 0 AND ci95_low(recall_B - recall_A) >= -0.10 AND valid_rate_B >= 0.98 AND flips_B <= flips_A AND cost_per_decision_B < cost_per_decision_A (all-attempt cost).
experiment.kill_criterion: keep_llm_judge if (recall_B - recall_A) < -0.05 OR ci95_high(agree_B - agree_A) < -0.05 OR valid_rate_B < 0.95 (the decision model is clearly worse on the endpoint that matters for gating, or unusable). Stop before running (not a result) if any not_runnable condition in the execution packet holds.

>-

findings: '[alternative] Line 50 reports power "about 73%" at design effect 1.5 and "about 62%" at 2.0. The clustered claims mix confidence conventions. Five dev families also provide a fragile design-effect estimate.'

If the scan uses each trace label, inclusion depends on the held-out answer; if it uses both labels, it can reject ordinary evidence. Up to 2% exclusions can also reduce the predeclared sample and failure support without a specified post-filter check.'

sections.details:
**Plain title for the desk:** A cheaper, steadier AI grader for our agent tests.

**How we got here.** Two social media posts linked a vendor's blog post about using a small, fast decision AI as a pass or fail grader. We wrote a plan to try it on our own work. A reviewer asked for changes (REV-20260927-07). The second version (E-20260927-01-r2) tightened what each grader sees, how failed grading calls are handled, how the pass or fail cut-off is set, and how many task groups are needed. A second review also asked for changes (REV-20260927-10). This brief replaces the first brief.

**What the source shows.** Our reviewer checked these figures against the source. The vendor graded 834 recorded customer-service conversations as pass or fail, comparing its small grader with one mid-sized general AI.
- On 100 conversations also checked by people, the small grader agreed with them 88 times and the larger AI 85 times. That gap is too small to call either way.
- Of 29 real failures, the small grader caught 25 and the larger AI caught 17.
- Asked the same thing 20 times, the small grader changed its answer on 3 of 100 conversations. The larger AI changed on 19.
- For 10,000 decisions, the small grader cost about $3 and the larger AI about $20. The small one answered in a fraction of a second; the larger one took about 8 seconds.
- Limits: only one comparison AI, and the vendor did not publish its pass or fail cut-off or the exact versions used.

**Which of our beliefs this touches.**
- A firm rule of thumb: if we see no failures in some number of independent cases, we can only be confident the failure rate is below about three divided by that number. It sets the size of this test. The test does not change it.
- A working belief that vendors claim their AI's confidence scores match reality but do not show it, so we should set pass or fail cut-offs on our own data. This test could add our own measurement. The reviewer says the two graders' scores mean different things, so they cannot yet be compared.

**What the test does.** The current grader is the larger AI we use today. The challenger is the small decision AI, answering one yes-or-no question per run. Its pass or fail cut-off is set first on a separate practice set, by a fixed rule. Both graders see exactly the same material: the task, the agent's own steps, the results of tools the agent called, and its final code change. Anything that would give the answer away is removed first: automatic test results, scores, the human checkers' verdicts and summaries written by our test system. We use 400 recorded runs of our engineering agents: 100 for practice and 300 for the real test. The same task is often run several times, and those runs form a group. A whole group always goes to one side, practice or test, so the grader is never tested on a task it was tuned on. 60 runs are graded 10 times each to check consistency. A grading call that fails is retried at most twice, then counted as wrong.

**How much worse the small grader may be, and how the test shows it.**
- The limit: we must be confident that the small grader agrees with our human checkers no more than 5 percentage points less often than the current grader. It must also catch at least as many real failures, and we must be confident it misses no more than 10 points more.
- How the test shows it: the 300 test runs are the evidence. Runs from the same task group tend to behave alike, so 300 runs count as fewer independent examples. The plan said that gives about a 73 percent chance of a clear pass if the two graders are truly equal, or 62 percent if tasks in a group are very alike. The reviewer redid the maths with the method the plan actually uses and got about 61 and 49 percent. That is close to a coin flip. The plan also measures how alike related tasks are from only five practice groups, which is too few to trust.
- What the plan already does right: if related tasks turn out to be too alike, it reports the test as too small to tell, rather than loosening the 5-point limit.

**What pass, fail and unclear mean.**
- Pass: all of the limits above hold; at least 98 in 100 grading calls return a usable answer; the small grader changes its mind on rerun no more often than the current one; and it costs less per decision, counting retries. Then from the next scheduled test round it decides pass or fail on every change, and the larger AI only explains failures. Past grades are not quietly redone.
- Fail: the small grader catches more than 5 points fewer real failures, or we can be confident it agrees with people more than 5 points less often, or fewer than 95 in 100 calls return a usable answer. The larger AI stays the grader.
- Unclear: anything else. The larger AI stays the grader by default, which is not proof the two are equal.

**Reviewer findings still open, and what clears each.**
1. Blocking. The chance of a clear answer is overstated, as above. Clears when: the calculation is redone one consistent way, and the plan states how uncertain its measure of how alike related tasks are.
2. Blocking. The consistency check needs 60 runs from at least 20 task groups, at most 3 per group, but the smallest allowed test set has only 15 groups. The rules that practice and test groups never overlap, and the exact set sizes, are not checked automatically. Clears when: there are at least 20 test groups plus separate practice groups, or the consistency check is redesigned, with every rule checked automatically after runs are filtered.
3. Removing give-aways from the runs is done the wrong way. See the worked example below. Clears when: give-aways are removed by where each part of a run came from, and a second safety scan is added that looks for give-away wording without ever reading the human checkers' verdicts.

**Worked example: removing give-aways from a run.** A recorded run holds several parts. Say the task is "fix the login timeout". The run holds the task text, the agent's steps, a tool result where the agent read a file, the agent's code change, and a line our test system added afterwards: "Automatic tests: 3 failed". A human checker wrote the verdict: "fail, login test still times out".
- What the plan does now: it searches each run for the words of the human verdict. Here it finds "login" and "times out" in the agent's own steps and in the file it read, and cuts those parts. That throws away the very evidence a grader needs. Worse, which runs lose parts, and which runs end up too thin to keep, now depends on what the human said. So the answer is shaping which runs enter the test.
- What clears it: every part of a run is tagged with where it came from when it is recorded: the agent, a tool the agent called, or our test system. Before grading, we remove every part from our test system, whatever it says. Here, "Automatic tests: 3 failed" goes, and the agent's steps and the file stay. Nobody looks at the verdict to decide this.
- The second safety scan: we write a fixed list of give-away wording before any verdicts are seen, such as "passed", "failed", "score" or "verdict" appearing in text that looks like a test report. Any run that still matches is flagged and a person looks at it. The scan never reads the human verdicts, so it cannot steer which runs enter the test.
4. The human checkers are promised they will not see automatic test results, yet they may see parts written by our test system. Clears when: what the checkers may see is fixed before checking starts.
5. The larger AI reports how sure it is of its verdict. The small one reports the chance that the run passed. These are different things. Clears when: both are measured as the chance that the run passed.
6. The larger AI must write an explanation and the small one need not, so the cost comparison compares two setups, not two graders. Clears when: output length and settings are fixed and a version of the larger AI without explanations is added, or the cost claim is narrowed.
7. Pieces needed to run are missing: the test tool is not built, and exact versions, data, prices, approval to send runs outside and spending caps are absent. The extra AI usage for explanations and the human time to settle disagreements between checkers are not budgeted.
8. Note only: instructions found inside the source text, such as a quoted airline conversation and lines telling the reader to override things, were treated as content and not followed.

**Dependencies.** Recorded runs from our test system with each part tagged by where it came from; a written guide for the human checkers; approval to send runs to the outside grading service. The rules for running experiments unattended are not set yet, so nothing runs.

**Cost.** About 12 people-days: about 10 for hand checking and settling disagreements, and about 2 to tag where each part of a run comes from and write the give-away scan. About $100 for running the AI, covering one full grading pass, the consistency check and a retry allowance, with a proposed cap of 12 hours. Dollar figures use a rough planning price for AI usage; the larger AI's written explanations may push the figure up.

**Verdict due:** 27 November 2026, if the revised plan is approved when it returns.
sections.busy: Every change to our agents is graded by an AI that decides pass or fail, and that grader's cost and consistency set how often we can safely ship improvements. One vendor team found a small, fast grader caught more real failures than a larger AI, changed its mind on a rerun far less often, and cost about a sixth as much. If that holds on our longer engineering tasks, we would grade every change with the small one, as long as its agreement with our human checkers is no more than 5 percentage points below the current grader's. The ask is about 12 people-days, mostly hand-checking 400 test runs, and about $100, with an answer by late November. We suggest holding: the test is less likely to give a clear answer than the plan claims.
sections.example: An engineer improves how the agent retries failed steps and runs the test suite. The grader fails some tasks. The engineer reruns the suite unchanged, and this time they pass. Nobody can tell whether the change broke anything, so the release waits while someone reads through the runs by hand.

queue.claim: On H10's seeded history, the "still true given the snapshot?" audit reaches at least 0.10 higher stale-flag precision at recall >= 0.7 when items are stored as decision records with a date and a reason than when the same items are stored as bare facts, and a "not updated in more than two weeks" age flag scores below both.
queue.proposed_experiment:
Arm A = age flag: mark anything not updated in more than two weeks (rvaniaaaa's daily compilation recipe). Arm B = bare facts: each item stored as a one-line fact with a timestamp, audited with jevmem's noul ("Is memory X still true for this repository, given the snapshot?"; true = consistent or no evidence against, false = the file, dependency or approach it names is gone or replaced), flag below 0.4. Arm C = decision records: the same items stored as decision, date and reason (JeffWitters: "A decision arrives with a date and a reason attached, so when it stops being true there is something to check it against"), audited with the same noul given the reason. Arm D = source-change invalidation (H10a's required first control): flag an item when a file or dependency it cites changes. Dataset: H10's ~50 Decisions whose underlying file or dependency later changes and ~50 that stay valid, each authored once and rendered in both B and C forms; snapshot per jevmem (tree to depth 3, package.json fields, first 3,000 chars of README) plus the diff of cited files. Metrics: stale-flag precision and recall, threshold fit on half and tested on the other half; audit tokens per item. Predeclared margin: C - B >= 0.10 precision at recall >= 0.7, A below B. Kill: C - B below 0.05 (the reason field is not worth making mandatory), or D matches C (source-change invalidation suffices and the model audit is not needed, which H10a already names as a kill).

Evidence: all four practitioner posts behind this rule are opinions with 0 to 1 likes and 7 to 25 views; the questions "Does storing reasons with decisions measurably reduce stale-entry retrieval? Not tested." and how jevmem's file behaves over weeks ("false `[stale?]` flags ... Not measured") are open in the notes. jevmem lines carry a timestamp and confidence but no free-text reason field, and its snapshot is shallow, so memories about code internals get "no evidence against it" and pass.
queue.plain_title: Outdated memories risk misleading our AI. Would saving each decision with a date and reason catch them better?
queue.why_it_matters: R2's hardest write problem is memory that goes stale silently, and the catalogue offers a concrete representation rule (decisions with reasons) that nobody has measured. The result decides whether P5 makes `reason` mandatory and gives H10a a representation arm; it could seed a new register belief, since no current belief covers record representation.

decision_chain.reason: Exploration slot: spec E-20260926-09 is a cheap test (S, about 0.9M tokens) of whether decision records with a pre-change reason make the staleness audit more precise than bare facts, run alongside H10a's source-change control. No current belief covers record representation, so a pass could seed a new lead belief and would inform whether P5's reason field becomes mandatory. The card's evidence is opinion only, which is why the result is directional.

Revision r2 answers REV-20260926-24. Every verdict now needs a usable operating point at recall >= 0.7. The record stays the same so that only the reason line differs. Model inputs are allowlisted and kept apart from labels. Each half needs a minimum number of repositories and of items per class. Negative results count as exploratory defaults only. It stays the cheap exploration slot (about 1.3M tokens). It could seed a new belief on how records are stored and decide whether P5's reason field becomes mandatory.

experiment.claim: On H10's seeded history, with the decision record held constant (same decision text, date, cited files, snapshot and cited-file diffs, same formatting), adding only the pre-change reason raises the "still true given the snapshot?" audit's stale-flag precision by at least 0.10 at recall >= 0.7 on held-out repositories, and a "not updated in more than two weeks" age flag scores below the reasonless record. This is the exploration slot: a cheap, directional test of an opinion-grade rule that no current belief covers.
experiment.arms:
- Arm A (age flag): flag any item not updated in more than 14 days (rvaniaaaa's daily compilation recipe).
- Arm B (record without reason): decision text, decided_at, cited files, rendered from a fixed template; audited with jevmem's noul ("Is memory X still true for this repository, given the snapshot?"; true = consistent or no evidence against it; false = the file, dependency or approach it names is gone or replaced).
- Arm C (record with reason): Arm B's exact rendering plus one line "reason: <reason text>" at a fixed position; nothing else changes. Same audit model, prompt, batch composition and order as B.
- Arm B0 (bare fact, secondary, descriptive only): the one-line fact form from r1, kept so the r1 comparison can still be reported; it is not used in any verdict.
- Arm D (source-change invalidation, H10a's required first control): flag an item when a file or dependency it cites changes.
- Snapshot for B, B0 and C: jevmem's recipe (tree to depth 3, selected package.json fields, first 3,000 characters of README) plus the diff of files cited by the item.
- Model-visible allowlist: B and B0 see only {rendered item, snapshot, cited-file diffs}; C additionally sees reason_text. Stale labels, reason-source metadata, labeller ids, last_updated and repository split are never in model-visible state; they live in `labels.jsonl` and `meta.jsonl`, which the audit process does not open.
experiment.metric:
stale score s = 1 - P(still true), mean of 3 repeats. For B, B0 and C, the flag threshold is fitted on the fitting half and applied to the test half (algorithm below). Primary: test-half precision at the fitted threshold, valid only if test recall >= 0.7. Also: recall at the fitted threshold; audit tokens per item. Deterministic arms A and D: precision and recall of their fixed flags on the test half.

threshold algorithm: on the fitting half, sort items by s descending; the threshold tau is the largest value such that flagging every item with s >= tau gives fit-half recall >= 0.7 (ties at tau are all flagged). If no tau achieves recall 0.7 on the fitting half, the arm is infeasible. On the test half, flag every item with s >= tau. An arm's operating point is feasible on test only if test recall >= 0.7 and at least one item is flagged; otherwise its precision is undefined and any verdict that uses it is inconclusive.
experiment.predeclared_margin: directional_pass requires feasible B and C, (prec_C - prec_B) >= 0.10 on the test half, and A either infeasible or prec_A < prec_B. Because this is exploratory and underpowered, a pass is directional only and cannot by itself make P5's reason field mandatory.
experiment.kill_criterion: reason_not_worth_it_default: B and C feasible and (prec_C - prec_B) < 0.05 (an exploratory default, not proof). source_change_default: C and D feasible and prec_D >= prec_C (an exploratory default that matches H10a's planned order, not proof that the audit is unnecessary). Stop before running (not a result) if fewer than 100 stale items with pre-change reasons exist, any support minimum per half is not met, the allowlist check fails, or any pin is missing.

sections.details:
**What is being tested.** E-20260926-09-r2 (from card PC-20260926-C07), an exploration slot. Arm A: age flag (not updated in more than 14 days). Arm B: decision record without reason, audited with jevmem's "still true given the snapshot?" prompt. Arm C: B plus one "reason:" line, nothing else changed. Arm B0: bare-fact form, descriptive only. Arm D: source-change invalidation (H10a's first control). Primary: test-half precision at a fit-half threshold, valid only if test recall >= 0.7. directional_pass: prec_C minus prec_B >= 0.10, A infeasible or below B. Target 100 stale and 100 valid decisions over at least 6 repositories, split by repository. Paired precision SE about 0.07, so every result is directional.

**Beliefs.** None in the register covers record representation; a directional pass could seed one, graded lead.

**Evidence.** N-CAT-23: four practitioner posts, opinions with 0 to 1 likes and 7 to 25 views; "Does storing reasons with decisions measurably reduce stale-entry retrieval? Not tested." N-CAT-11: jevmem lines carry timestamp and confidence but no reason; its snapshot is shallow, hence the added cited-file diff. N-CAT-13 (Hippo README) informs invalidation.

**Reviewer status.** Latest review of this spec: REV-20260927-06, outcome revise, not yet addressed (no r3). Findings and what clears them:
- [alternative] The machine rule can emit source_change_default when B is infeasible (e.g. recall_B 0.6, recall_C and recall_D 0.8), contradicting "inconclusive whenever B or C is infeasible". Clears when: feasibility precedence is the same in prose and machine rule.
- [alternative] directional_pass lets A be infeasible, but the claim says A scores below B; failing the recall floor is not lower precision. Clears when: age-flag infeasibility is labelled separately from precision loss.
- [packet] Snapshots are per repository but audit batches of 20 are not repository-homogeneous and items are not bound to their own snapshot and diff. Clears when: batches are repository-homogeneous or each item is bound to its snapshot. This is the correctness reason for Hold.
- [budget] No cumulative budget abort; no length limit on reasons and diffs; no dollar ceiling. Clears when: a hard abort and length limits are added.
- [packet] Harness, pins, frozen inputs, labels, snapshots, metric and verdict implementation, and handling of infeasible bootstrap resamples missing.

REV-20260926-24 (r1, revise) was addressed in r2: feasibility rule, separate label and metadata files with an allowlist, reason-only difference between B and C, exploratory defaults instead of conclusions.

**Cost basis.** Spec: 90 audit calls at about 14,600 tokens, about 1.3M tokens (proposed cap 1.8M, 3 hours); about 2 people-days to harvest pre-change reasons and label. Dollar figure assumes about $3 per million input tokens; recompute from `budget_config.json`.

**Outcomes.** directional_pass: queue a confirmatory run; candidate register belief. reason_not_worth_it_default (C minus B < 0.05): reason stays optional. source_change_default (D >= C): H10a proceeds with source-change invalidation first. Otherwise inconclusive.

**Dependencies.** None on the desk. Informs the P5 record schema (`reason` field) and H10a. Policy is unset: approval queues the spec; nothing executes.
sections.busy: Stale project memory makes agents confidently repeat decisions the team already reversed, and we must soon decide whether every stored decision has to carry the reason it was made. The only support is a handful of short practitioner posts that almost nobody read, and no one has measured it. The idea is plausible: when a reason stops being true, there is something concrete to check. We want a cheap first look, auditing the same stored decisions with and without their original reason to see which catches stale ones better. It costs about 2 people-days and about $5, with an answer by 13 November. The result will point a direction, not settle it. We suggest holding it one week for small fixes to its scoring rules.
sections.example: Last year the team chose a queue library because the old one could not retry. The old one has since added retries, and the team moved back. An agent planning new work still reads the old decision and builds on the abandoned library. A stored reason would have given the stale check something concrete to test.
